entries.bfa47c19b7e50579fcd758eb089b950c1e71674b: <div sID="gen3631" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Deut.16" sID="Deut.16"/> <div eID="gen3631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3632" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3633" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A repetition of the laws concerning the three yearly feasts; in particular, that of the passover, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.1-Deut.16.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. That of pentecost, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.9-Deut.16.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. That of tabernacles, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.13-Deut.16.15">ver. 13-15</reference>. And the general law concerning the people's attendance on them, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.16-Deut.16.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>. II. The institution of an inferior magistracy, and general rules of justice given to those that were called into office, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.18-Deut.16.20">ver. 18-20</reference>. III. A caveat against groves and images, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.21-Deut.16.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>.
entries.46f31559629d810d9977114824ab30eeb147bc0a: <div eID="gen3633" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3632" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Yearly Release. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3634" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Observe the month of Abib, and keep the passover unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God: for in the month of Abib the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God brought thee forth out of Egypt by night. <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou shalt therefore sacrifice the passover unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, of the flock and the herd, in the place which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall choose to place his name there. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thou shalt eat no leavened bread with it; seven days shalt thou eat unleavened bread therewith, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the bread of affliction; for thou camest forth out of the land of Egypt in haste: that thou mayest remember the day when thou camest forth out of the land of Egypt all the days of thy life. <hi type="super">4</hi> And there shall be no leavened bread seen with thee in all thy coast seven days; neither shall there <hi type="italic">any thing</hi> of the flesh, which thou sacrificedst the first day at even, remain all night until the morning. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thou mayest not sacrifice the passover within any of thy gates, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee: <hi type="super">6</hi> But at the place which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God shall choose to place his name in, there thou shalt sacrifice the passover at even, at the going down of the sun, at the season that thou camest forth out of Egypt. <hi type="super">7</hi> And thou shalt roast and eat <hi type="italic">it</hi> in the place which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God shall choose: and thou shalt turn in the morning, and go unto thy tents. <hi type="super">8</hi> Six days thou shalt eat unleavened bread: and on the seventh day <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a solemn assembly to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God: thou shalt do no work <hi type="italic">therein.</hi> <hi type="super">9</hi> Seven weeks shalt thou number unto thee: begin to number the seven weeks from <hi type="italic">such time as</hi> thou beginnest <hi type="italic">to put</hi> the sickle to the corn. 10 And thou shalt keep the feast of weeks unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God with a tribute of a freewill offering of thine hand, which thou shalt give <hi type="italic">unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God,</hi> according as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath blessed thee: <hi type="super">11</hi> And thou shalt rejoice before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy manservant, and thy maidservant, and the Levite that <hi type="italic">is</hi> within thy gates, and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, that <hi type="italic">are</hi> among you, in the place which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath chosen to place his name there. <hi type="super">12</hi> And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt: and thou shalt observe and do these statutes. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou shalt observe the feast of tabernacles seven days, after that thou hast gathered in thy corn and thy wine: 14 And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast, thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy manservant, and thy maidservant, and the Levite, the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, that <hi type="italic">are</hi> within thy gates. <hi type="super">15</hi> Seven days shalt thou keep a solemn feast unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God in the place which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall choose: because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God shall bless thee in all thine increase, and in all the works of thine hands, therefore thou shalt surely rejoice. <hi type="super">16</hi> Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles: and they shall not appear before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> empty: <hi type="super">17</hi> Every man <hi type="italic">shall give</hi> as he is able, according to the blessing of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God which he hath given thee. <div eID="gen3634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3635" type="x-p"/> Much of the communion between God and his people Israel was kept up, and a face of religion preserved in the nation, by the three yearly feasts, the institution of which, and the laws concerning them, we have several times met with already; and here they are repeated. <div eID="gen3635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3636" type="x-p"/> I. The law of the passover, so great a solemnity that it made the whole month, in the midst of which it was placed, considerable: <hi type="italic">Observe the month Abib,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.16.1">v. 1</reference>. Though one week only of this month was to be kept as a festival, yet their preparations before must be so solemn, and their reflections upon it and improvements of it afterwards so serious, as to amount to an observance of the whole month. The month of Abib, or of <hi type="italic">new fruits,</hi> as the Chaldee translates it, answers to our March (or part of March and part of April), and was by a special order from God, in remembrance of the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt, made the <hi type="italic">beginning of their year</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.2">Exod. xii. 2</reference>), which before was reckoned to begin in September. This month they were to keep the passover, in remembrance of their being <hi type="italic">brought out of Egypt by night,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.16.1">v. 1</reference>. The Chaldee paraphrasts expound it, "Because they came out of Egypt by daylight," there being an express order that they should not stir out of their doors till morning, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.22">Exod. xii. 22</reference>. One of them expounds it thus: "<hi type="italic">He brought thee out of Egypt,</hi> and did wonders <hi type="italic">by night.</hi>" The other, "and thou shalt eat the passover <hi type="italic">by night.</hi>" The laws concerning it are, 1. That they must be sure to sacrifice the passover in the place that God should choose (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.2">v. 2</reference>), and in no other place, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.5-Deut.16.7">v. 5-7</reference>. The passover was itself a sacrifice; hence Christ, as our passover, is said to be <hi type="italic">sacrificed for us</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">1 Cor. v. 7</reference>), and many other sacrifices were offered during the seven days of the feast (<reference osisRef="Num.28.19">Num. xxviii. 19</reference>, &c.), which are included here, for they are said to be sacrificed <hi type="italic">of the flock and the herd,</hi> whereas the passover itself was only of the flock, either a lamb or a kid: now no sacrifice was accepted but from the altar that sanctified it; it was therefore necessary that they should go up to the place of the altar, for, though the paschal lamb was entirely eaten by the owners, yet it must be killed in the court, the blood sprinkled, and the inwards burned upon the altar. By confining them to the appointed rule, from which they would have been apt to vary, and to introduce foolish inventions of their own, had they been permitted to offer these sacrifices within their own gates, from under the inspection of the priests. They were also hereby directed to have their eye up unto God in the solemnity, and the <hi type="italic">desire of their hearts towards the remembrance of his name,</hi> being appointed to attend where he had chosen <hi type="italic">to place his name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.16.2">v. 2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.16.6">6</reference>. But, when the solemnity was over, they might <hi type="italic">turn and go unto their tents,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.16.7">v. 7</reference>. Some think that they might, if they pleased, return the very morning after the paschal lamb was killed and eaten, the priests and Levites being sufficient to carry on the rest of the week's work; but the first day of the seven is so far from being the day of their dispersion that it is expressly appointed for a <hi type="italic">holy convocation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.7">Lev. xxiii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.28.18">Num. xxviii. 18</reference>); therefore we must take it as Jonathan's paraphrase expounds it, <hi type="italic">in the morning after the end of the feast thou shalt go to thy cities.</hi> And it was the practice to keep together the whole week, <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.17">2 Chron. xxxv. 17</reference>. 2. That they must eat unleavened bread for seven days, and no leavened bread must be seen in all their coasts, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.3-Deut.16.4">v. 3, 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.8">8</reference>. The bread they were confined to is here called <hi type="italic">bread of affliction,</hi> because neither grateful to the taste nor easy of digestion, and therefore proper to signify the heaviness of their spirits in their bondage and to keep in remembrance the haste in which they came out, the case being so urgent that they could not stay for the leavening of the bread they took with them for their march. The Jewish writers tell us that the custom at the passover supper was that the master of the family broke this unleavened bread, and gave to every one a piece of it, saying, <hi type="italic">This is</hi> (that is, this signifies, represents, or commemorates, which explains that saying of our Saviour, <hi type="italic">This is my body</hi>) <hi type="italic">the bread of affliction which your fathers did eat in the land of Egypt.</hi> The gospel meaning of this feast of unleavened bread the apostle gives us, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">1 Cor. v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Christ our passover being sacrificed for us,</hi> and we having participated in the blessed fruits of that sacrifice to our comfort, <hi type="italic">let us keep the feast</hi> in a holy conversation, free from <hi type="italic">the leaven of malice</hi> towards our brethren and hypocrisy towards God, and <hi type="italic">with the unleavened bread of sincerity</hi> and love. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Observe, concerning the passover, for what end it was instituted: "<hi type="italic">That thou mayest remember the day when thou camest forth out of Egypt,</hi> not only on the day of the passover, or during the seven days of the feast, but <hi type="italic">all the days of thy life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.3">v. 3</reference>), as a constant inducement to obedience." Thus we celebrate the memorial of Christ's death at certain times, that we may remember it at all times, as a reason why we should <hi type="italic">live to him that died for us and rose again.</hi> <div eID="gen3636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3637" type="x-p"/> II. Seven weeks after the passover the feast of pentecost was to be observed, concerning which they are here directed, 1. Whence to number their seven weeks, <hi type="italic">from the time thou beginnest to put the sickle to the corn</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.9">v. 9</reference>), that is, from the morrow after the first day of the feast of unleavened bread, for on that day (though it is probable the people did not begin their harvest till the feast was ended) messengers were sent to reap a sheaf of barley, which was to be offered to God as the first-fruits, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.10">Lev. xxiii. 10</reference>. Some think it implies a particular care which Providence would take of their land with respect to the weather, that their harvest should be always ripe and ready for the sickle just at the same time. 2. How they were to keep this feast. (1.) They must <hi type="italic">bring an offering unto God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.16.10">v. 10</reference>. It is here called a <hi type="italic">tribute of a free-will-offering.</hi> It was required of them as a tribute to their Sovereign Lord and owner, under whom they held all they had; and yet because the law did not determine the <hi type="italic">quantum,</hi> but it was left to every man's generosity to bring what he chose, and whatever he brought he must give cheerfully, it is therefore called a <hi type="italic">free-will offering.</hi> It was a grateful acknowledgment of the goodness of God to them in the mercies of these corn-harvests now finished, and therefore must be <hi type="italic">according as God had blessed them.</hi> Where God sows plentifully he expects to reap accordingly. (2.) They must rejoice before God, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.11">v. 11</reference>. Holy joy is the heart and soul of thankful praises, which are as the language and expression of holy joy. They must rejoice in their receivings from God, and in their returns of service and sacrifice to him; our duty must be our delight as well as our enjoyments. They must have their very servants to rejoice with them, "for remember (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.12">v. 12</reference>) that <hi type="italic">thou wast a bond-man,</hi> and wouldest have been very thankful if thy taskmasters would have given thee some time and cause for rejoicing; and thy God did bring thee out to keep a feast with gladness; therefore be pleasant with thy servants, and make them easy." And, it should seem, those general words, <hi type="italic">thou shalt observe and do these statutes,</hi> are added here for a particular reason, because this feast was kept in remembrance of the giving of the law upon Mount Sinai, fifty days after they came out of Egypt; now the best way of expressing our thankfulness to God for his favour to us in giving us his law is to <hi type="italic">observe and do according to the precepts</hi> of it. <div eID="gen3637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3638" type="x-p"/> III. They must keep the feast of tabernacles, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.13-Deut.16.15">v. 13-15</reference>. Here is no repetition of the law concerning the sacrifices that were to be offered in great abundance at this feast (which we had at large, <reference osisRef="Num.29.12">Num. xxix. 12</reference>, &c.), because the care of these belonged to the priests and Levites, who had not so much need of a repetition as the people had, and because the spiritual part of the service, which consisted in holy joy, was most pleasing to God, and was to be the perpetual duty of a gospel conversation, of which this feast was typical. Observe what stress is laid upon it here: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt rejoice in thy feast</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">and, because the Lord shall bless thee, thou shalt surely rejoice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.16.15">v. 15</reference>. Note, 1. It is the will of God that his people should be a cheerful people. If those that were under the law must rejoice before God, much more must we that are under the grace of the gospel, which makes it our duty, not only as here to rejoice in our feasts, but to <hi type="italic">rejoice evermore, to rejoice in the Lord always.</hi> 2. When we rejoice in God ourselves we should do what we can to assist others also to rejoice in him, by comforting the mourners and supplying the necessitous, that even <hi type="italic">the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow may rejoice with us.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Job.29.13">Job xxix. 13</reference>. 3. We must rejoice in God, not only because of what we have received and are receiving from him daily, but because of what he has promised, and we expect to receive yet further from him: because <hi type="italic">he shall bless thee,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">thou shalt rejoice.</hi> Those that make God their joy may <hi type="italic">rejoice in hope,</hi> for he is faithful that has promised. <div eID="gen3638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3639" type="x-p"/> IV. The laws concerning the three solemn feasts are summed up (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.16-Deut.16.17">v. 16, 17</reference>), as often before, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Exod. xxiii. 16, 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.23">xxxiv. 23</reference>. The general commands concerning them are, 1. That all the males must then make their personal appearance before God, that by their frequent meeting to worship God, at the same place, and by the same rule, they might be kept faithful and constant to that holy religion which was established among them. 2. That none must appear before God empty, but every man must bring some offering or other, in token of a dependence upon God and gratitude to him. And God was not unreasonable in his demands; let every man but give as he was able, and no more was expected. The same is still the rule of charity, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1 Cor. xvi. 2</reference>. Those that give to their power shall be accepted, but those that give beyond their power are accounted worthy of double honour (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.3">2 Cor. viii. 3</reference>), as the poor widow that gave <hi type="italic">all she had,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.21.4">Luke xxi. 4</reference>.
entries.12b612603342a3c6ffdc00a884a7d93d3a3f30ad: <div eID="gen3639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3640" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment. <hi type="super">19</hi> Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous. <hi type="super">20</hi> That which is altogether just shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee. <hi type="super">21</hi> Thou shalt not plant thee a grove of any trees near unto the altar of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, which thou shalt make thee. <hi type="super">22</hi> Neither shalt thou set thee up <hi type="italic">any</hi> image; which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hateth. <div eID="gen3640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3641" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Care taken for the due administration of justice among them, that controversies might be determined, matters in variance adjusted, the injured redressed, and the injurious punished. While they were encamped in the wilderness, they had <hi type="italic">judges and officers</hi> according to their numbers, rulers of thousands and hundreds, <reference osisRef="Exod.17.25">Exod. xvii. 25</reference>. When they came to Canaan, they must have them according to their towns and cities, in all their gates; for the courts of judgment sat in the gates. Now, 1. Here is a commission given to these inferior magistrates: "Judges to try and pass sentence, and officers to execute their sentences, shalt thou make thee." However the persons were pitched upon, whether by the nomination of their sovereign or by the election of the people, <hi type="italic">the power were ordained of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1">Rom. xiii. 1</reference>. And it was a great mercy to the people thus to have justice brought to their doors, that it might be more expeditious and less expensive, a blessing which we of this nation ought to be very thankful for. Pursuant to this law, besides the great sanhedrim that sat at the sanctuary, consisting of seventy elders and a president, there was in the larger cities, such as had in them above 120 families, a court of twenty-three judges, in the smaller cities a court of three judges. See this law revived by Jehoshaphat, <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.5">2 Chron. xix. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.8">8</reference>. 2. Here is a command given to these magistrates to do justice in the execution of the trust reposed in them. Better not judge at all than not judge with just judgment, according to the direction of the law and the evidence of the fact. (1.) The judges are here cautioned not to do wrong to any (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.19">v. 19</reference>), nor to take any gifts, which would tempt them to do wrong. This law had been given before, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.8">Exod. xxiii. 8</reference>. (2.) They are charged to do justice to all: "<hi type="italic">That which is altogether just shalt thou follow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.16.20">v. 20</reference>. Adhere to the principles of justice, act by the rules of justice, countenance the demands of justice, imitate the patterns of justice, and pursue with resolution that which appears to be just. <hi type="italic">Justice, justice, shalt thou follow.</hi>" This is that which the magistrate is to have in his eye, on this he must be intent, and to this all personal regards must be sacrificed, to do <hi type="italic">right to all</hi> and <hi type="italic">wrong to none.</hi> <div eID="gen3641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3642" type="x-p"/> II. Care taken for the preventing of all conformity to the idolatrous customs of the heathen, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.21-Deut.16.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. They must not only not join with the idolaters in their worships, not visit their groves, nor bow before the images which they had set up, but, 1. They must not plant a grove, nor so much as a tree, near God's altar lest they should make it look like the altars of the false gods. They made groves the places of their worship either to make it secret (but that which is true and good desires the light rather), or to make it solemn, but the worship of the true God has enough in itself to make it so and needs not the advantage of such a circumstance. 2. They must not set up any image, statue, or pillar, to the honour of God, for it is a thing which the Lord hates; nothing belies or reproaches him more, or tends more to corrupt and debauch the minds of men, than representing and worshipping by an image that God who is an infinite and eternal Spirit.  <chapter eID="Deut.16"/> <div eID="gen3642" type="x-p"/>

entries.50e81eeb3e76166216c409df65d7d2e360532acc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1793"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.16.1-Deut.16.22">De 16:1-22</reference>. The Feast of the Passover.</title> <div sID="gen2402" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1793"/><hi type="bold">1. Observe the month of Abib--</hi>or first-fruits. It comprehended the latter part of our March and the beginning of April. Green ears of the barley, which were then full, were offered as first-fruits, on the second day of the passover.<div eID="gen2402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2403" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for in the month of Abib the Lord thy God brought thee out of Egypt by night--</hi>This statement is apparently at variance with the prohibition (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.22">Ex 12:22</reference>) as well as with the recorded fact that their departure took place in the morning (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.3">Ex 13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.33.3">Nu 33:3</reference>). But it is susceptible of easy reconciliation. Pharaoh's permission, the first step of emancipation, was extorted during the night, the preparations for departure commenced, the rendezvous at Rameses made, and the march entered on in the morning. <div eID="gen2403" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e7160ed930eb6cc5527cffe47e19ac5a6fbdf67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1794"/><div sID="gen2404" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1794"/><hi type="bold">2. Thou shalt therefore sacrifice the passover--</hi>not the paschal lamb, which was strictly and properly the passover. The whole solemnity is here meant, as is evident from the mention of the additional victims that required to be offered on the subsequent days of the feast (<reference osisRef="Num.28.18">Nu 28:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.28.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.8">2Ch 35:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.9">9</reference>), and from the allusion to the continued use of unleavened bread for seven days, whereas the passover itself was to be eaten at once. The words before us are equivalent to "thou shalt observe the feast of the passover." <div eID="gen2404" type="x-p"/>
entries.20f5555a1a81ec1171a052bd5bdc0e0f633f0c18: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1795"/><div sID="gen2405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1795"/><hi type="bold">3. seven days shalt thou eat unleavened bread--</hi>a sour, unpleasant, unwholesome kind of bread, designed to be a memorial of their Egyptian misery and of the haste with which they departed, not allowing time for their morning dough to ferment. <div eID="gen2405" type="x-p"/>
entries.75ad6a9b2c53261348c77e7b424a61b3932efb38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1796"/><div sID="gen2406" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1796"/><hi type="bold">5-6. Thou mayest not sacrifice the passover within any of thy gates--</hi>The passover was to be observed nowhere but in the court of the tabernacle or temple, as it was not a religious feast or sacramental occasion merely, but an actual sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.27">Ex 12:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.18">23:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.25">34:25</reference>). The blood had to be sprinkled on the altar and in the place where the true Passover was afterwards to be sacrificed for us "at even, at the going down of the sun"--literally, "between the evenings." <div eID="gen2406" type="x-p"/>
entries.b463405a1191ede5e1b778385d45b5bdfaca6439: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1798"/><div sID="gen2408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1798"/><hi type="bold">7. thou shalt roast and eat it--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Exod.12.8">Ex 12:8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.13">2Ch 35:13</reference>).<div eID="gen2408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2409" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt turn in the morning, and go unto thy tents--</hi>The sense of this passage, on the first glance of the words, seems to point to the morning after the first day--the passover eve. Perhaps, however, the divinely appointed duration of this feast, the solemn character and important object, the journey of the people from the distant parts of the land to be present, and the recorded examples of their continuing all the time (<reference osisRef="2Chr.30.21">2Ch 30:21</reference> <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.17">35:17</reference>), (though these may be considered extraordinary, and therefore exceptional occasions), may warrant the conclusion that the leave given to the people to return home was to be on the morning after the completion of the seven days. <div eID="gen2409" type="x-p"/>
entries.92e5afcf92c19817b151df6d64db31301fe4961e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1799"/><div sID="gen2410" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1799"/><hi type="bold">9-12. Seven weeks shalt thou number--</hi>The feast of weeks, or a WEEK OF WEEKS: the feast of pentecost (see on <reference osisRef="Lev.23.10">Le 23:10</reference>; also see <reference osisRef="Exod.34.22">Ex 34:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.1">Ac 2:1</reference>). As on the second day of the passover a sheaf of new barley, reaped on purpose, was offered, so on the second day of pentecost a sheaf of new wheat was presented as first-fruits (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Ex 23:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.28.26">Nu 28:26</reference>), a freewill, spontaneous tribute of gratitude to God for His temporal bounties. This feast was instituted in memory of the giving of the law, that spiritual food by which man's soul is nourished (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.3">De 8:3</reference>). <div eID="gen2410" type="x-p"/>
entries.f92dc6e7edef73664293be2f396e56d7a82cc09f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1800"/><div sID="gen2411" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1800"/><hi type="bold">13-17. Thou shalt observe the feast of tabernacles seven days--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Exod.23.14">Ex 23:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.34">Le 23:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.29.12">Nu 29:12</reference>). Various conjectures have been formed to account for the appointment of this feast at the conclusion of the whole harvest. Some imagine that it was designed to remind the Israelites of the time when they had no cornfields to reap but were daily supplied with manna; others think that it suited the convenience of the people better than any other period of the year for dwelling in booths; others that it was the time of Moses' second descent from the mount; while a fourth class are of opinion that this feast was fixed to the time of the year when the Word was made flesh and dwelt--literally, "tabernacled"--among us (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>), Christ being actually born at that season. <div eID="gen2411" type="x-p"/>
entries.2000fad69f9bdabfd5385f697f12b57430394f41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1803"/><div sID="gen2414" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1803"/><hi type="bold">18-20. Judges and officers shalt thou make--</hi>These last meant heralds or bailiffs, employed in executing the sentence of their superiors.<div eID="gen2414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2415" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all thy gates--</hi>The gate was the place of public resort among the Israelites and other Eastern people, where business was transacted and causes decided. The Ottoman Porte derived its name from the administration of justice at its gates. <div eID="gen2415" type="x-p"/>
entries.26698cecbc05817ec722c890f08ac062711f38cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1804"/><div sID="gen2416" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1804"/><hi type="bold">21. Thou shalt not plant thee a grove--</hi>A grove has in Scripture a variety of significations--a group of overshadowing trees, or a grove adorned with altars dedicated to a particular deity, or a wooden image in a grove (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.25">Jud 6:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4-2Kgs.23.6">2Ki 23:4-6</reference>). They might be placed near the earthen and temporary altars erected in the wilderness, but they could not exist either at the tabernacle or temples. They were places, which, with their usual accompaniments, presented strong allurements to idolatry; and therefore the Israelites were prohibited from planting them. <div eID="gen2416" type="x-p"/>
entries.22f634997618d85f51f01bd301c7d30c90610511: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1805"/><div sID="gen2417" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1805"/><hi type="bold">22. Neither shalt thou set thee up any image--</hi>erroneously rendered so for "pillar"; pillars of various kinds, and materials of wood or stone were erected in the neighborhood of altars. Sometimes they were conical or oblong, at other times they served as pedestals for the statues of idols. A superstitious reverence was attached to them, and hence they were forbidden. <chapter eID="Deut.16"/>

entries.63d6efbfdc80fbc94483594207d5d6e8712aa425: <div eID="gen6749" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6750" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6751" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6751" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6750" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6752" type="x-p"/> The month of Abib to be observed, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.1">Deu 16:1</reference>. The feast of the passover and of unleavened bread, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.2-Deu.16.8">Deu 16:2-8</reference>. The feast of weeks, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.9-Deu.16.12">Deu 16:9-12</reference>. The feast of tabernacles, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.13-Deu.16.15">Deu 16:13-15</reference>. All the males to appear before the Lord thrice in the year, none to come empty, each to give according to his ability, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.16">Deu 16:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.17">Deu 16:17</reference>. Judges and officers to be made in all their cities, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.18">Deu 16:18</reference>. Strict justice shall be executed, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.19">Deu 16:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.20">Deu 16:20</reference>. No grove to be planted near the altar of God, nor any image to be set up, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.21">Deu 16:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.22">Deu 16:22</reference>. <div eID="gen6752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6753" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen6753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6754" type="x-p"/> Keep the passover - A feast so called because the angel that destroyed the firstborn of the Egyptians, seeing the blood of the appointed sacrifice sprinkled on the lintels and door-posts of the Israelites' houses, passed over Them, and did not destroy any of their firstborn. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.12.2">Exo 12:2</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exo.12.3">Exo 12:3</reference> (note), etc.
entries.e17cdf9e1bbcf1115f6bf56868d840fcca0c4493: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen6754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6755" type="x-p"/> Bread of affliction - Because, being baked without leaven, it was unsavoury, and put them in mind of their afflictive bondage in Egypt.
entries.c420d1f3b5403b2238048199271d65a83f8a5ca0: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen6755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6756" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt rejoice - The offerings of the Israelites were to be eaten with festivity, communicated to their friends with liberality, and bestowed on the poor with great generosity, that they might partake with them in these repasts with joy before the Lord. To answer these views it was necessary to eat the flesh while it was fresh, as in that climate putrefaction soon took place; therefore they were commanded to let nothing remain until the morning, <reference osisRef="Deu.16.4">Deu 16:4</reference>. This consideration is sufficient to account for the command here, without having recourse to those moral and evangelical reasons that are assigned by the learned and devout Mr. <div eID="gen6756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6757" type="x-p"/> Ainsworth for the command. How beneficent and cheerful is the design of this institution! - Harmer, vol. i., p. 396.
entries.d80b407048a31ffe465b56d4fd9914df63d2fd5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen6757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6758" type="x-p"/> Three times in a year - See <reference osisRef="Exo.23.14">Exo 23:14</reference> (note), where all the Jewish feasts are explained. See also <reference osisRef="Lev.23.34">Lev 23:34</reference> (note).
entries.8021b7249e023b279ec49fe7805d2801db74694c: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen6758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6759" type="x-p"/> Judges and officers shalt thou make - Judges, שפטים shophetim, among the Hebrews, were probably the same as our magistrates or justices of the peace. Officers, שטרים shoterim, seem to have been the same as our inquest sergeants, beadles, etc., whose office it was to go into the houses, shops, etc., and examine weights, measures, and the civil conduct of the people. When they found any thing amiss, they brought the person offending before the magistrate, and he was punished by the officer on the spot. They seem also to have acted as heralds in the army, <reference osisRef="Deu.20.5">Deu 20:5</reference>. See also Rab. Maimon in Sanhedrin. In China, for all minor offenses, the person when found guilty is punished on the spot, in the presence of the magistrate or mandarin of justice.
entries.3442aa753db7701488ce37db247faaff0603fb7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen6759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6760" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not plant thee a grove, etc. - We have already seen that groves were planted about idol temples for the purpose of the obscene worship performed in them. (See on <reference osisRef="Deu.12.3">Deu 12:3</reference> (note)). On this account God would have no groves or thickets about his altar, that there might be no room for suspicion that any thing contrary to the strictest purity was transacted there. Every part of the Divine worship was publicly performed, for the purpose of general edification.  <chapter eID="Deut.16"/> <div eID="gen6760" type="x-p"/>

entries.cca72af0a5c59b930d5d838327714a49d5a85ddc: <reference osisRef="Deut.16.1-Deut.16.8">Deu 16:1-8</reference> <div eID="gen2340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2341" type="x-p"/> Israel was to make ready the Passover to the Lord in the earing month (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.12.2">Exo 12:2</reference>). The precise day is supposed to be known from Ex 12, as in Exo 23:15. פּסח עשׂה (<hi type="italic">to prepare the Passover</hi>), which is used primarily to denote the preparation of the paschal lamb for a festal meal, is employed here in a wider signification viz., “<hi type="italic">to keep the Passover</hi>.” At this feast they were to slay sheep and oxen to the Lord for a Passover, at the place, etc. In <reference osisRef="Deut.16.2">Deu 16:2</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.16.1">Deu 16:1</reference>, the word “Passover” is employed in a broader sense, and includes not only the paschal lamb, but the paschal sacrifices generally, which the Rabbins embrace under the common name of <hi type="italic">chagiga</hi>; not the burnt-offerings and sin-offerings, however, prescribed in Num 28:19-26, but all the sacrifices that were slain at the feast of the Passover (i.e., during the seven days of the <hi type="italic">Mazzoth</hi>, which are included under the name of <hi type="italic">pascha</hi>) for the purpose of holding sacrificial meals. This is evident from the expression “of the flock and the herd;” as it was expressly laid down, that only a שׂה, i.e., a yearling animal of the sheep or goats, was to be slain for the paschal meal on the fourteenth of the month in the evening, and an ox was never slaughtered in the place of the lamb. But if any doubt could exist upon this point, it would be completely set aside by <reference osisRef="Deut.16.3">Deu 16:3</reference> : “<hi type="italic">Thou shalt eat no leavened bread with it: seven days shalt thou eat unleavened bread therewith</hi>.” As the word “therewith” cannot possibly refer to anything else than the “Passover” in <reference osisRef="Deut.16.2">Deu 16:2</reference>, it is distinctly stated that the slaughtering and eating of the Passover was to last seven days, whereas the Passover lamb was to be slain and consumed in the evening of the fourteenth Abib (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.10">Exo 12:10</reference>). Moses called the unleavened bread “<hi type="italic">the bread of affliction</hi>,” because the Israelites had to leave Egypt in anxious flight (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.11">Exo 12:11</reference>) and were therefore unable to leaven the dough (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.39">Exo 12:39</reference>), for the purpose of reminding the congregation of the oppression endured in Egypt, and to stir them up to gratitude towards the Lord their deliverer, that they might remember that day as long as they lived. (On the meaning of the <hi type="italic">Mazzothy</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Exod.12.8">Exo 12:8</reference> and Exo 12:15.) - On account of the importance of the unleavened bread as a symbolical shadowing forth of the significance of the Passover, as the feast of the renewal and sanctification of the life of Israel, Moses repeats in <reference osisRef="Deut.16.4">Deu 16:4</reference> two of the points in the law of the feast: first of all the one laid down in <reference osisRef="Exod.13.7">Exo 13:7</reference>, that no leaven was to be seen in the land during the seven days; and secondly, the one in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.18">Exo 23:18</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exod.34.25">Exo 34:25</reference>, that none of the flesh of the paschal lamb was to be left till the next morning, in order that all corruption might be kept at a distance from the paschal food. Leaven, for example, sets the dough in fermentation, from which putrefaction ensues; and in the East, if flesh is kept, it very quickly decomposes. He then once more fixes the time and place for keeping the Passover (the former according to <reference osisRef="Exod.12.6">Exo 12:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.23.5">Lev 23:5</reference>, etc.), and adds in <reference osisRef="Deut.16.7">Deu 16:7</reference> the express regulation, that not only the slaughtering and sacrificing, but the roasting (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.12.9">Exo 12:9</reference>) and eating of the paschal lamb were to take place at the sanctuary, and that the next morning they could turn and go back home. This rule contains a new feature, which Moses prescribes with reference to the keeping of the Passover in the land of Canaan, and by which he modifies the instructions for the first Passover in Egypt, to suit the altered circumstances. In Egypt, when Israel was not yet raised into the nation of Jehovah, and had as yet no sanctuary and no common altar, the different houses necessarily served as altars. But when this necessity was at an end, the slaying and eating of the Passover in the different houses were to cease, and they were both to take place at the sanctuary before the Lord, as was the case with the feast of Passover at Sinai (Num 9:1-5). Thus the smearing of the door-posts with the blood was tacitly abolished, since the blood was to be sprinkled upon the altar as sacrificial blood, as it had already been at Sinai. - The expression “<hi type="italic">to thy tents</hi>,” for going “home,” points to the time when Israel was till dwelling in tents, and had not as yet secured any fixed abodes and houses in Canaan, although this expression was retained at a still later time (e.g., <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.2">1Sa 13:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.9">2Sa 19:9</reference>, etc.). The going home in the morning after the paschal meal, is not to be understood as signifying a return to their homes in the different towns of the land, but simply, as even <hi type="italic">Riehm</hi> admits, to their homes or lodgings at the place of the sanctuary. How very far Moses was from intending to release the Israelites from the duty of keeping the feast for seven days, is evident from the fact that in <reference osisRef="Deut.16.8">Deu 16:8</reference> he once more enforces the observance of the seven days’ feast. The two clauses, “six days thou shalt eat <hi type="italic">mazzoth</hi>,” and “on the seventh day shall be <hi type="italic">azereth</hi> (Eng. Ver. 'a solemn assembly') to the Lord thy God,” are not placed in antithesis to each other, so as to imply (in contradiction to <reference osisRef="Deut.16.3">Deu 16:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.16.4">Deu 16:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.12.18-Exod.12.19">Exo 12:18-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.13.6-Exod.13.7">Exo 13:6-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.6">Lev 23:6</reference>; Num 28:17) that the feast of Mazzoth was to last only six days instead of seven; but the seventh day is brought into especial prominence as the <hi type="italic">azereth</hi> of the feast (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.23.36">Lev 23:36</reference>), simply because, in addition to the eating of <hi type="italic">mazzoth</hi>, there was to be an entire abstinence from work, and this particular feature might easily have fallen into neglect at the close of the feast. But just as the eating of mazzoth for seven days is not abolished by the first clause, so the suspension of work on the first day is not abolished by the second clause, any more than in <reference osisRef="Exod.13.6">Exo 13:6</reference> the first day is represented as a working day by the fact that the seventh day is called “a feast to Jehovah.”
entries.1b8247da8297e9a07a61938ed14e7c2a6925a8b2: <reference osisRef="Deut.16.9-Deut.16.12">Deu 16:9-12</reference> <div eID="gen2341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2342" type="x-p"/> With regard to the Feast of Weeks (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Exo 23:16</reference>), it is stated that the time for its observance was to be reckoned from the Passover. Seven weeks shall they count “<hi type="italic">from the beginning of the sickle to the corn</hi>,” i.e., from the time when the sickle began to be applied to the corn, or from the commencement of the corn-harvest. As the corn-harvest was opened with the presentation of the sheaf of first-fruits on the second day of the Passover, this regulation as to time coincides with the rule laid down in Lev 23:15. “<hi type="italic">Thou shalt keep the feast to the Lord thy God according to the measure of the free gift of thy hand, which thou givest as Jehovah thy God blesseth thee</hi>.” The ἁπ. λεγ. מסּת is the standing rendering in the Chaldee for דּי, sufficiency, need; it probably signifies abundance, from מסס = מסה, to flow, to overflow, to derive. The idea is this: Israel was to keep this feast with sacrificial gifts, which every one was able to bring, according to the extent to which the Lord had blessed him, and (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.11">Deu 16:11</reference>) to rejoice before the Lord at the place where His name dwelt with sacrificial meals, to which the needy were to be invited (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.14.29">Deu 14:29</reference>), in remembrance of the fact that they also were bondmen in Egypt (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.15.15">Deu 15:15</reference>). The “<hi type="italic">free-will offering of the hand</hi>,” which the Israelites were to bring with them to this feast, and with which they were to rejoice before the Lord, belonged to the free-will gifts of burnt-offerings, meat-offerings, drink-offerings, and thank-offerings, which might be offered, according to Num 29:39 (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.23.38">Lev 23:38</reference>), at every feast, along with the festal sacrifices enjoined upon the congregation. The latter were binding upon the priests and congregation, and are fully described in Num 28 and 29, so that there was no necessity for Moses to say anything further with reference to them.
entries.e0269f6fecac8d11f7c9d161fea115de96aaec42: <reference osisRef="Deut.16.13-Deut.16.15">Deu 16:13-15</reference> <div eID="gen2342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2343" type="x-p"/> In connection with the Feast of Tabernacles also, he simply enforces the observance of it at the central sanctuary, and exhorts the people to rejoice at this festival, and not only to allow their sons and daughters to participate in this joy, but also the man-servant and maid-servant, and the portionless Levites, strangers, widows, and orphans. After what had already been stated, Moses did not consider it necessary to mention expressly that this festal rejoicing was also to be manifested in joyous sacrificial meals; it was enough for him to point to the blessing which God had bestowed upon their cultivation of the corn, the olive, and the vine, and upon all the works of their hands, i.e., upon their labour generally (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.13-Deut.16.15">Deu 16:13-15</reference>), as there was nothing further to remark after the instructions which had already been given with reference to this feast also (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.34-Lev.23.36">Lev 23:34-36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.39-Lev.23.43">Lev 23:39-43</reference>; Num 29:12-38).
entries.141dcd1ac16e69345d30a1eb4752d73894c341ad: <reference osisRef="Deut.16.16-Deut.16.17">Deu 16:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen2343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2344" type="x-p"/> In conclusion, the law is repeated, that the men were to appear before the Lord three times a year at the three feasts just mentioned (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.23.17">Exo 23:17</reference> with <reference osisRef="Exod.23.14">Exo 23:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exod.34.23">Exo 34:23</reference>), with the additional clause, “<hi type="italic">at the place which the Lord shall choose</hi>,” and the following explanation of the words “not empty:” “<hi type="italic">every man according to the gift of his hand, according to the blessing of Jehovah his God, which He hath given thee</hi>,” i.e., with sacrificial gifts, as much as every one could offer, according to the blessing which he had received from God. <div eID="gen2344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2345" type="x-p"/> Just as in its religious worship the Israelitish nation was to show itself to be the holy nation of Jehovah, so was it in its political relations also. This thought forms the link between the laws already given and those which follow. Civil order - that indispensable condition of the stability and prosperity of nations and states - rests upon a conscientious maintenance of right by means of a well-ordered judicial constitution and an impartial administration of justice. - For the purpose of settling the disputes of the people, Moses had already provided them with judges at Sinai, and had given the judges themselves the necessary instructions for the fulfilment of their duties (Ex 18). This arrangement might suffice as long as the people were united in one camp and had Moses for a leader, who could lay before God any difficult cases that were brought to him, and give an absolute decision with divine authority. But for future times, when Israel would no longer possess a prophet and mediator like Moses, and after the conquest of Canaan would live scattered about in the towns and villages of the whole land, certain modifications and supplementary additions were necessary to adapt this judicial constitution to the altered circumstances of the people. Moses anticipates this want in the following provisions, in which he <hi type="italic">first</hi> of all commands the appointment of judges and officials in every town, and gives certain precise injunctions as to their judicial proceedings (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.18-Deut.17.7">Deut 16:18-17:7</reference>); and <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, appoints a higher judicial court at the place of the sanctuary for the more difficult cases (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.8-Deut.17.13">Deu 17:8-13</reference>); and <hi type="italic">thirdly</hi>, gives them a law for the future with reference to the choice of a king (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.14-Deut.16.20">Deu 16:14-20</reference>).
entries.9686ea1c4da10a1824151bb6944174fbac25326c: <reference osisRef="Deut.16.18-Deut.16.20">Deu 16:18-20</reference> <div eID="gen2345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2346" type="x-p"/> Appointment and Instruction of the Judges. - Deu 16:18. “<hi type="italic">Judges and officers thou shalt appoint thee in all thy gates</hi> (place, see at <reference osisRef="Exod.20.10">Exo 20:10</reference>), <hi type="italic">which Jehovah thy God shall give thee, according to thy tribes</hi>.” The nation is addressed as a whole, and directed to appoint for itself judges and officers, i.e., to choose them, and have them appointed by its rulers, just as was done at Sinai, where the people chose the judges, and Moses inducted into office the persons so chosen (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.1.12-Deut.1.18">Deu 1:12-18</reference>). That the same course was to be adopted in future, is evident from the expression, “throughout thy tribes,” i.e., according to thy tribes, which points back to Deu 1:13. Election by majorities was unknown to the Mosaic law. The <hi type="italic">shoterim</hi>, officers (lit., writers, see at <reference osisRef="Exod.5.6">Exo 5:6</reference>), who were associated with the judges, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.1.15">Deu 1:15</reference>, even under the previous arrangement, were not merely messengers and servants of the courts, but secretaries and advisers of the judges, who derived their title from the fact that they had to draw up and keep the genealogical lists, and who are mentioned as already existing in Egypt as overseers of the people and of their work (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.5.6">Exo 5:6</reference>; and for the different opinions concerning their official position, see <hi type="italic">Selden, de Synedriis,</hi> i. pp. 342-3). The new features, which Moses introduces here, consist simply in the fact that every place was to have its own judges and officers, whereas hitherto they had only been appointed for the larger and smaller divisions of the nation, according to their genealogical organization. Moses lays down no rule as to the number of judges and <hi type="italic">shoterim</hi> to be appointed in each place, because this would depend upon the number of the inhabitants; and the existing arrangement of judges over tens, hundreds, etc. (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.21">Exo 18:21</reference>), would still furnish the necessary standard. The statements made by <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Rabbins</hi> with regard to the number of judges in each place are contradictory, or at all events are founded upon the circumstances of much later times (see my <hi type="italic">Archäologie</hi>, ii. pp. 257-8). - These judges were to judge the people with just judgment. The admonition in <reference osisRef="Deut.16.19">Deu 16:19</reference> corresponds to the instructions in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.6">Exo 23:6</reference> and Exo 23:8. “Respect persons:” as in Deu 1:17. To this there is added, in <reference osisRef="Deut.16.20">Deu 16:20</reference>, an emphatic admonition to strive zealously to maintain justice. The repetition of the word justice is emphatic: justice, and nothing but justice, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.10">Gen 14:10</reference>, etc. But in order to give the people and the judges appointed by them a brief practical admonition, as to the things they were more especially to observe in their administration of justice, Moses notices by way of example a few crimes that were deserving of punishment (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.21">Deu 16:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.22">Deu 16:22</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.17.1">Deu 17:1</reference>), and then proceeds in <reference osisRef="Deut.17.2-Deut.17.7">Deu 17:2-7</reference> to describe more fully the judicial proceedings in the case of idolaters.
entries.c5be9bae626be7dd304039b4e7da6eda06a6a6f3: <reference osisRef="Deut.16.21">Deu 16:21</reference> <div eID="gen2346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2347" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Thou shalt not plant thee as asherah any wood beside the altar of Jehovah</hi>.” נטע, to plant, used figuratively, to plant up or erect, as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.11">Ecc 12:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.25">Dan 11:25</reference>; cf. Isa 51:16. <hi type="italic">Asherah</hi>, the symbol of <hi type="italic">Astarte</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.34.13">Exo 34:13</reference>), cannot mean either a green tree or a grove (as <hi type="italic">Movers, Relig. der Phönizier, </hi>p. 572, supposes), for the simple reason that in other passages we find the words עשׂה, make (1Ki 14:15; 1Ki 16:33; 2Ki 17:16; 2Ki 21:3; <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.3">2Ch 33:3</reference>), or הצּיב, set up (2Ki 17:10), העמיד, stand up (<reference osisRef="2Chr.33.19">2Ch 33:19</reference>), and בּנה, build (1Ki 14:23), used to denote the erection of an <hi type="italic">asherah</hi>, not one of which is at all suitable to a tree or grove. But what is quite decisive is the fact that in 1Ki 14:23; 2Ki 17:10; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.2">Jer 17:2</reference>, the <hi type="italic">asherah</hi> is spoken of as being set up under, or by the side of, the green tree. This idol generally consisted of a wooden column; and a favourite place for setting it up was by the side of the altars of Baal.

entries.2fcdcb38b197ca94585366dbf9390310b948ce2f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.16.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.16.1" sID="gen14220" type="section"/> <div sID="gen14221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Observe the month Abib.</hi> For what purpose God instituted the Passover, has already been shewn in the exposition of the First Commandment; for since it was a symbol of redemption, and in that ceremony the people exercised themselves in the pure worship of the One God, so as to acknowledge Him to be their only Father, and to distinguish Him from all idols, I thought that the actual slaying of the lamb should be introduced amongst the Supplements to the First Commandment. It only remains for us to speak here of what relates to the Sabbath. This then was the first solemn day, on which God would have His people rest and go up to Jerusalem, forsaking all their business. But mention is here made not only of the Paschal Lamb, but He also commands sheep and oxen to be slain in the place which He should choose. In these words He signifies that on that day a holy convocation was to be held; which is soon after more clearly expressed, for I have already given the two intermediate verses in the institution of the Passover itself, He therefore prohibits their slaying the Passover apart in their own cities, but would have them all meet in the same sanctuary. It has been elsewhere said that one altar was prescribed for them, as if God would gather them under one banner for the preservation of concord and the unity of the faith. What is added respecting the solemnity of the seventh day is very appropriate to this place.<div eID="gen14221" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.16.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen14220" osisID="Deut.16.1" type="section"/>

Deuteronomy 16:3 Thou shalt eat no leavened bread with it. Because by this sign they were reminded of their having escaped in haste, as it were from the very flames; therefore does Moses so often enforce the prohibition of leaven. And here this reason for it is alleged, viz., that their recollection should be recalled to the affliction from which they were rescued; for they must needs have been involved in the greatest straits, when there was no time even for baking bread. Unleavened bread is therefore called “the bread of affliction,” that the manner of their deliverance may the more enhance God’s grace. He repeats what we have seen before, that none of the flesh of the Lamb should be reserved to the following day. In the former passage from the Book of Exodus, because Moses speaks generally, the command may at first sight be referred to the perpetual sacrifice; but the latter passage takes away all obscurity, by the express mention of the passover. We need not wonder that in one place the word “fat” is used for the whole carcase, or any part of the lamb, either by synecdoche, or that God might commend the superior sanctity of the fat, of which they were not permitted to eat, and which was burnt in all sacrifices.

entries.0e4928900d4b41d76cb9bcf530e337edddefc942: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.16.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.16.9" sID="gen14222" type="section"/> <div sID="gen14223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> <hi type="italic">Seven weeks shalt thou number.</hi> It must be observed that the Passover fell in a part of the year when the harvests were beginning to ripen; and consequently the first-fruits, of which I treated under the First Commandment, were then offered. Seven weeks afterwards they celebrated another feast-day, which was called Pentecost, <hi type="italic">i.e., </hi>the fiftieth, by the Greeks. There was just this number of days between the departure of the people and the publication of the Law. Another offering of first-fruits was then made, in which each one, according to his ability, and in proportion to the produce of the year, consecrated a gift to God of the harvested fruits. In order that they might be more ready and cheerful in their liberality, God’s blessing is set before them, as if Moses had commanded the people to testify their gratitude; since whatever springs from the earth, is the mere bounty of God Himself.<div eID="gen14223" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.16.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen14222" osisID="Deut.16.9" type="section"/>
entries.86a000e56a07b3a5c65f60ce50eef898ab2a6a3b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.16.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.16.11" sID="gen14224" type="section"/> <div sID="gen14225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> <hi type="italic">And thou shalt require.</hi> On another ground he exhorts and excites them to willingness, because the service of God brings this rejoicing; for there is nothing which ought more to stimulate us to obedience, that when we know that God rather consults our good than seeks to obtain any advantage from us. Ungodly men, indeed, rejoice also, nay, they are wanton and intemperate in their joy; but since that joy is not only transient, but their laughter is turned into weeping and gnashing of teeth, it is not without cause that Moses here magnifies it as a peculiar blessing, to rejoice before God; as if a father should invite his children to delight themselves together with him. But by this external exercise, believers were reminded that there is no real or desirable joy, unless in reference to God. And surely, however the wicked may exult in their pleasures, and abandon themselves to gratifcations, still, since tranquillity of conscience, which alone brings true rejoicing, is wanting to them, they do not enjoy the merriment into which they plunge themselves. Finally, Moses amplifies by a comparison the good which they enjoyed in the service of God, when he says, “And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt;” for that their present condition might be more pleasant to them, he heightened its sweetness by the recollection of their most miserable captivity. Quoest </hi>iv., “<foreign xml:lang="la">Nam cum ratione animus movetur placide et constanter, tum illud <hi type="italic">gaudium </hi>dicitur; cum autem inaniter, et effuse animus exultat, tum ilia <hi type="italic">laetitia </hi>gestiens, vel nimia dici potest; quam ita definiunt, sine ratione animi elationem</foreign>.” —<hi type="italic"> Edit. Elz., </hi>1661, p. 1088, a.<div eID="gen14226" type="x-p"/> </note> very subtle distinction between the words <hi type="italic">gaudium </hi>and <hi type="italic">laetitia, </hi>for unless I take both of them in a good sense, I could not translate the Hebrew words, whereby God would express how indulgently He deals with His children. 18. Judges and officers shalt thou make. I have placed this passage among the Supplements of the Fifth Commandment, for, if it pleases God that judges should be appointed for ruling the people, it follows that their laws and edicts should be obeyed; and thus the parental authority extends also to them. But, in order that the people may more readily submit themselves to judges, God reminds them that the human race could not otherwise be preserved. Public utility, therefore, renders the authority of magistrates pleasant and agreeable, though it would else be hateful. But, although it be not conceded to all to elect their judges, because God honored His chosen people with this prerogative, still he here recommends in general a regular government, since He signifies that human society cannot hold together unless the lawful rulers have authority to execute justice. Whether, then, magistrates are appointed by the suffrages of the people, or imposed in any other way, let us learn that they are the necessary ministers of God, to confine all men under the yoke of the laws. The latter passage, which I have annexed from Deuteronomy 7, refers to the same thing, viz., that even in war discipline is necessary, lest all things should be thrown into confusion. Now, if it pleases God that certain superior officers should have the command, it follows that they must be obeyed; for it would be ridiculous to appoint governors, if it were lawful to despise them with impunity. When, therefore, God sets military commanders over the people, He enforces the duty of humble submission.
